structure.title: Thought and discussion
structure.text: The opening states the problem of social power; the defence of open discussion tests the authority to silence an opinion.

structure.title: Lives and limits
structure.text: Later chapters defend individuality, examine society's authority over conduct, and consider practical applications.

people.name: Individuality
people.text: The development of a person's capacities and choices.

context.title: Disapproval and coercion
context.text: Mill distinguishes judging conduct from being entitled to prevent it. The distinction becomes difficult when actions affect several people.

context.title: Fallible majorities
context.text: A widely accepted opinion can still be mistaken or poorly understood. Discussion serves knowledge even when an objection ultimately fails.

notice.why: Liberty protects experiments that respectable opinion finds unattractive.
The principle's scope depends on distinctions about agency and social obligation.

opening: A whole society agrees that an opinion is dangerous, foolish, or disgusting. John Stuart Mill asks what gives it the right to silence the person who holds it. His defence of liberty extends beyond unpopular speech to unpopular ways of living, where neighbours can enforce conformity without ever calling the police. The argument becomes most demanding when tolerance costs something: when the person being protected seems wrong, the experiment looks reckless, and everyone respectable would feel more comfortable if it stopped.
